clinicalPearls: At least 1.4 million U.S. adults are living with congenital heart disease (CHD); the majority were diagnosed in childhood, but a substantial percentage have CHD first recognized in adulthood, so lifelong follow-up with ACHD expertise is recommended (Harrison 22e p.2067).

ASD physiology is predominantly a left-to-right shunt; the degree of shunting (and thus right heart volume loading) depends on defect size and the diastolic properties of the heart. As patients age, diabetes, hypertension, and atherosclerosis reduce left-heart compliance and may increase left-to-right shunting and symptoms (Harrison 22e p.2070).

The classic ASD physical finding is a wide, FIXED splitting of the second heart sound, due to prolonged RV ejection and increased pulmonary artery capacitance delaying pulmonary valve closure; the ECG commonly shows incomplete right bundle branch block (Harrison 22e p.2070).

Secundum ASD (defect in the region of the fossa ovalis) is the most common type and can often be closed percutaneously with an occluder device; a patent foramen ovale (PFO) is distinct, is NOT associated with right-sided dilation, and persists in up to 25% of adults (Harrison 22e p.2070).

Surgical closure (not percutaneous) is required for primum ASDs, sinus venosus defects, and coronary sinus septal defects; a sinus venosus defect is not actually a defect of the atrial septum but a communication near the SVC- or IVC-atrial junction with right pulmonary veins (Harrison 22e p.2070-2071).

VSDs are the most common congenital anomaly recognized at birth but account for only ~10% of adult CHD, owing to the high rate of spontaneous closure of small VSDs in early life; the most common location is the membranous (perimembranous/outlet) septum (Harrison 22e p.2071-2072).

Outcome for adults with small VSDs WITHOUT ventricular dilation or pulmonary hypertension is generally excellent; small muscular defects persisting into adulthood are often pressure- and flow-restricted with no significant hemodynamic consequence (Harrison 22e p.2072).

Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common form of cyanotic CHD (~0.5 per 1000 live births) and comprises anterior conal-septal deviation causing RV outflow tract obstruction, a VSD, RV hypertrophy, and an overriding aorta (Harrison 22e p.2073).

In repaired tetralogy of Fallot, pulmonary regurgitation is common and is usually associated with RV dilation; accurate quantification of RV size, function, and mass is particularly important because RV dilation, dysfunction, and hypertrophy are associated with adverse outcomes, and cardiac MRI is routinely used for surveillance (Harrison 22e p.2073-2074).

Eisenmenger syndrome is the consequence of a long-standing high-volume or pressurized left-to-right shunt: excessive pulmonary blood flow leads to severely increased pulmonary vascular resistance that eventually REVERSES the shunt, creating bidirectional or right-to-left flow and cyanosis; it can complicate any CHD with an initial left-to-right shunt (Harrison 22e p.2078).

Selective pulmonary vasodilators such as bosentan or sildenafil are efficacious in Eisenmenger syndrome; select patients may be candidates for combined heart-lung transplantation, or preferably lung transplantation with concomitant repair of the intracardiac defect when feasible (Harrison 22e p.2078).

Endocarditis prophylaxis before dental procedures is advised in high-risk CHD lesions: unrepaired cyanotic CHD (including palliative shunts/conduits), completely repaired defects during the first 6 months after repair, and repaired CHD with residual defects adjacent to prosthetic material (Harrison 22e p.745, Table 133-9).
harrison.pathophysiology: The normal heart is analyzed segmentally (atria, ventricles, great arteries joined by the atrioventricular canal and conus), with attention to alignment (what drains into what) and connection (how segments are physically linked). The heart forms from the third week of gestation and is nearly complete by 8 weeks; cardiac neural crest cells migrating in weeks 5-6 are essential for outflow septation, semilunar valve formation, and aortic arch patterning, so disturbance of these processes underlies conotruncal defects. Shunt lesions are defined by the relative compliance, pressure, and outflow resistance of the connected chambers/vessels and the defect size. Left-to-right shunts (ASD, VSD, PDA) move oxygenated blood toward the deoxygenated (right) side, volume-loading the pulmonary circulation: ASD/PAPVR (proximal to the tricuspid valve) cause right heart dilation, whereas VSD/PDA (below the tricuspid valve) cause left heart dilation. Sustained high-volume or pressurized left-to-right shunting can raise pulmonary vascular resistance to the point that the shunt reverses (Eisenmenger physiology, right-to-left, cyanosis). Tetralogy of Fallot produces a right-to-left shunt across the VSD because RV outflow obstruction raises right-sided systolic pressure, mixing deoxygenated blood into the LV and causing systemic arterial cyanosis. In transposition of the great arteries the aorta arises from the RV and the pulmonary artery from the LV, creating parallel rather than series circulations that are incompatible with life unless mixing exists (ASD, VSD, or PDA).
additionalDifferentials: Atrial septal defect (secundum, primum, sinus venosus, coronary sinus types) - most common cause of right heart dilation from a shunt
Patent foramen ovale (distinct from ASD; not associated with right heart dilation)
Ventricular septal defect (membranous/perimembranous, muscular, AV-canal/inlet, subpulmonary/conal types)
Ebstein anomaly of the tricuspid valve
Tetralogy of Fallot (most common cyanotic CHD)
Transposition of the great arteries (D-loop and congenitally corrected L-loop)
Coarctation of the aorta (with associated bicuspid aortic valve)
Single ventricle physiology (tricuspid atresia, double inlet LV, hypoplastic left heart) post-Fontan
Eisenmenger syndrome (any unrepaired left-to-right shunt that has reversed)
nonInfectiousMimics: Atrial septal defect may be mistaken for mitral stenosis; features favoring ASD over MS include a pulmonary mid-to-upper left sternal border flow murmur, and large left-to-right shunts can produce findings overlapping with MS (Harrison 22e p.2065 / Chap. on MS).
Arrhythmogenic RV cardiomyopathy and Uhl's anomaly are non-shunt myocardial causes of right heart dilation that can mimic the dilated right heart of an ASD.
additionalInvestigations: Transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography with agitated saline (bubble) contrast - needed to diagnose PFO and non-secundum ASDs; color flow Doppler for VSDs and shunt-ratio estimation
Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging - routine surveillance of RV size, function, and mass in repaired tetralogy of Fallot and other complex CHD; cross-sectional imaging detects PAPVR

Surface ECG - incomplete right bundle branch block in ASD; QRS duration >=180 ms in repaired TOF flags risk of ventricular tachycardia/sudden death; ventricular pre-excitation (WPW) in up to 20% of Ebstein anomaly
Cardiac catheterization - shunt quantification and hemodynamic assessment, particularly when pulmonary hypertension is suspected

Genetic evaluation - testing for 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge) in conotruncal defects (clues: right aortic arch, aberrant subclavian artery); recognition of trisomy 21, Noonan (PTPN11), Williams (7q11.23), and Turner syndromes
Fetal echocardiogram between 18 and 22 weeks of gestation for pregnant patients with CHD
redFlags: Reversal of a left-to-right shunt to right-to-left flow with cyanosis = Eisenmenger syndrome; develops from severely elevated pulmonary vascular resistance and is a multi-organ condition
Right heart dilation in an unrepaired ASD without other cause signals risk of progression to symptomatic right heart failure, atrial arrhythmias, and pulmonary arterial hypertension
QRS duration >=180 ms on resting ECG in repaired tetralogy of Fallot - associated with increased risk of ventricular tachycardia and sudden cardiac death
Systemic RV dysfunction after atrial switch (Mustard/Senning) for D-loop TGA - the most worrisome long-term complication, with no proven effective medical therapy

Pregnancy in a woman with Eisenmenger syndrome is contraindicated due to high risk of maternal mortality; pulmonary arterial hypertension and severe systemic ventricular dysfunction are WHO class IV (extremely high maternal risk)
New exercise-capacity decline in ACHD may be unrecognized by the patient; by the time symptoms appear, irreversible physiologic changes may already have occurred
harrison.prognosis: Outcomes vary widely by lesion. Adults with small VSDs without ventricular dilation or pulmonary hypertension generally have an excellent prognosis. Repaired coarctation patients generally do well but remain at risk for systemic hypertension, premature atherosclerosis, LV failure, and aortic aneurysm/dissection and recoarctation. In repaired tetralogy of Fallot, one prospective cohort of 144 adults showed 72% survival at 40 years but only 25% cumulative event-free survival (events: reintervention, most commonly pulmonary valve replacement; symptomatic arrhythmia; heart failure); LV dysfunction is present in at least 20%. The arterial switch operation for D-loop TGA has produced substantial long-term survival, whereas atrial switch leaves a systemic RV prone to dysfunction. Adults with Eisenmenger syndrome have significant morbidity but generally survive longer than patients with other forms of pulmonary arterial hypertension. In aggregate, adults with CHD have quality-of-life-limiting comorbidities and premature mortality far exceeding age-matched controls, and nearly all can be classified as stage A heart failure or greater; care within a center that has an ACHD specialty program is associated with improved overall survival.
pitfalls: Confusing a PFO (flap-valve patency, present in up to 25% of adults, no right heart dilation) with a true secundum ASD.

Assuming all ASDs are amenable to percutaneous closure - large defects, inadequate tissue rims, and anomalous draining pulmonary veins make device closure unfavorable, and primum/sinus venosus/coronary sinus defects require surgery.
Overlooking that a sinus venosus defect is not in the atrial septum itself, so it may be missed without dedicated imaging.

Routine phlebotomy in an asymptomatic adult with Eisenmenger syndrome is contraindicated; elevated hematocrit appropriate to the degree of cyanosis should not be lowered reflexively, and iron deficiency should be corrected because it impairs quality of life and function.

Using teratogenic medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, direct oral anticoagulants, endothelin receptor blockers) in CHD patients of childbearing potential; estrogen-containing contraception should be avoided in Eisenmenger syndrome due to thrombogenicity.
Failing to test adults with conotruncal defects for 22q11 deletion (DiGeorge) - many were never tested, and unrecognized cognitive/psychiatric disability may go untreated.
Treating an ACHD patient's seemingly minor lesion without recognizing limited hemodynamic reserve and subclinical multi-organ dysfunction before noncardiac surgery.
harrison.severityClassification: The chapter applies the modified World Health Organization (mWHO) classification of maternal risk in heart disease during pregnancy, graded mWHO I (no detectable increased mortality risk, e.g., small/mild lesions) through mWHO IV (extremely high maternal mortality risk; pregnancy generally contraindicated). Examples by class: mWHO II includes unoperated ASD/VSD and repaired tetralogy of Fallot; mWHO III includes mechanical valve, systemic RV, and Fontan circulation; mWHO IV includes pulmonary arterial hypertension, severe systemic ventricular dysfunction (EF <30% or NYHA III-IV), severe aortic dilatation, and Fontan with any complication. The CARPREG II weighted-risk score is also described (highest 3-point factors: prior cardiac event/arrhythmia, NYHA >=III, mechanical valve), stratifying predicted cardiac-event risk from 5% (<=1 point) to 41% (>4 points). For repaired tetralogy of Fallot, potential sequelae are catalogued in Table 280-3 and long-term sequelae of D-loop TGA surgery in Table 280-4.
